[{"element":"menu_content","data":{"key":"menu_content_deployment","id":"menu_content_deployment","name":"menu_content_deployment"},"elements":[{"node":"deploy_overview","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Overview","key":"deploy_overview","id":"deploy_overview","name":"deploy_overview","value":"# Deployment

Loopar is multi-tenant from the ground up, and it runs as **a single process — the core**. The same layout serves a laptop and a production server: one core, many tenants, Caddy in front.

![Loopar single-core multi-tenant architecture](/assets/public/home-multitenant.svg)

| Piece | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Core** (`loopar-core`) | One Node process, one port (`config/core.json` → `port`, default 3000). Resolves every request to its tenant by host name |
| **Tenants** | `sites/<name>/` — own database, config, users, domain. Turned on or off inside the core |
| **dev site** | The default tenant, where you build apps and manage the others |
| **PM2** | Keeps the core alive — a **project-local** daemon (`.pm2/`) driven by the `yarn` CLI |
| **Caddy** | Routes every tenant domain to the core; automatic SSL for public domains |

> **Key concept:** development or production is a **global** mode of the core (`config/core.json` → `nodeEnv`). Every tenant runs in the same mode.
"}},{"node":"deploy_core","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Core & Mode","key":"deploy_core","id":"deploy_core","name":"deploy_core","value":"## The Core and Its Mode

Server-wide settings live in `config/core.json` — nothing per tenant:

```json
{
  "port": 3000,
  "nodeEnv": "development",
  "host": "0.0.0.0",
  "caddy": { "acmeEmail": null },
  "redis": { "host": null, "port": 6379 }
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|-----|---------|
| `port` | The single HTTP port of the core — every domain routes here |
| `nodeEnv` | `development` (Vite middleware, HMR) or `production` (prebuilt bundle) |
| `host` | Bind address |
| `caddy.acmeEmail` | Email for Let's Encrypt certificates |
| `redis` | Optional shared cache |
| `debug` | Force the Debugger on (`true`) or off; by default it follows the mode |

Every getter falls back to an environment variable and then a default, so a missing `core.json` never breaks boot.

### Switching the mode

| From | How |
|------|-----|
| Terminal | `yarn prod` (needs a build) · `m` in the TUI |
| Desk | **Tenant Manager** → **Core: Dev / Prod** |

The core restarts to apply the change.
"}},{"node":"deploy_tm","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Tenant Manager","key":"deploy_tm","id":"deploy_tm","name":"deploy_tm","value":"## Tenant Manager

Manage tenants from the **Tenant Manager** in the Desk of your dev site, or from the terminal with the **TUI** (`yarn start`).

### Creating a Tenant

| Field | Required | Example |
|-------|----------|--------|
| **Name** | ✅ | `client-abc` → `sites/client-abc/` |
| **Domain** | ❌ | `client-abc.localhost` or `client.com` |
| **Websites** | ❌ | One per line: `shop.client.com = shop` (domain = app) |

Save, then **Open** it: the tenant's install wizard asks for the database, organization and Administrator. There is no port to pick — each tenant is also reachable at `<name>.localhost` on the core's port.

### Actions

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Open** | The tenant's Desk, or its install link while it isn't installed |
| **Start / Stop** | Turn the tenant on or off. Off tenants serve a suspended page; data is kept |
| **Restart** | Re-initialize the tenant (configuration and apps) |
| **Reset** | Drop its database and return to the install wizard |
| **Destroy** | Remove the tenant: database, `sites/<name>/`, Caddy route (asks for its name) |
| **Build / Deploy** | Full rebuild, or promote `build/staging` to a live release |
| **Core: Dev / Prod** | Switch the core's global mode |

You can't stop the tenant you are working in — use another tenant's Desk or the TUI.

### From the terminal

```bash
yarn tenant list
yarn tenant on client-abc
yarn tenant off client-abc
```
"}},{"node":"deploy_caddy","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Domains & Caddy","key":"deploy_caddy","id":"deploy_caddy","name":"deploy_caddy","value":"## Domains & Caddy

Caddy is a **catch-all** in front of the core: every tenant domain (and every website domain) is routed to the core's single port, and the core picks the tenant by host.

```
client.localhost ─┐
demo.localhost   ─┼──► Caddy ──► core :3000 ──► Host → tenant
client.com       ─┘     (SSL)
```

### Development domains (`.localhost`)

`<tenant>.localhost` works without DNS — browsers resolve `.localhost` to `127.0.0.1`. In development Caddy tries `:80` (so URLs need no port) and otherwise falls back to a free port.

### Production domains

Point the domain's DNS to the server, set it as the tenant's **Domain** (or as one of its **Websites**) and save. Loopar updates Caddy through its Admin API (`localhost:2019`) and Caddy obtains the certificate. In production Caddy must listen on `:80`/`:443` — Loopar fails loudly instead of silently serving elsewhere.

You never edit a Caddyfile by hand.

### Installing Caddy

```bash
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install -y debian-keyring debian-archive-keyring apt-transport-https curl
curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/gpg.key' | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/caddy-stable-archive-keyring.gpg
curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/debian.deb.txt' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-stable.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install caddy

# macOS
brew install caddy
```

On Linux, let Caddy bind low ports without root (once):

```bash
sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' $(which caddy)
```

### Behind Cloudflare

Use SSL mode **Full** so Cloudflare talks HTTPS to Caddy. During a restart Cloudflare shows its own error page for a few seconds.
"}},{"node":"deploy_pm2","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Processes","key":"deploy_pm2","id":"deploy_pm2","name":"deploy_pm2","value":"## Processes (PM2)

PM2 keeps the core alive. Loopar runs a **project-local daemon** (state under `.pm2/` in the project), so it never mixes with other PM2 installs on the machine. Drive it through the CLI:

```bash
yarn serve               # boot the core headless, in the configured mode
yarn restart             # restart the core
yarn stop                # stop the core
yarn logs                # tail every process (yarn logs loopar-core for one)
yarn startup             # boot hook: start Loopar after a reboot (run once)
yarn kill                # stop everything, daemon included
```

| Process | When |
|---------|------|
| `loopar-core` | Always — serves every tenant |
| `build-watch` | Only while `yarn watch` keeps `build/staging` fresh |

The core runs a single instance on purpose: scheduled jobs, naming-series counters and realtime live in that process. Scale up the machine, not the instance count.
"}},{"node":"deploy_build","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Builds & Releases","key":"deploy_build","id":"deploy_build","name":"deploy_build","value":"## Builds & Releases

In production the core serves a prebuilt bundle from `dist`, a symlink to the current release.

```
dist -> build/releases/<tag>   # what the server serves
build/
  releases/<tag>/              # versioned, immutable releases
  staging/                     # output of yarn watch, source for fast deploys
```

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `yarn build` | Full build: new release → client + server bundles (compressed) → atomic activation |
| `yarn watch` | Background builder (`build-watch`): incremental rebuilds into `build/staging/` |
| `yarn activate` | Snapshot `build/staging/` into a new release and activate it (fast deploy) |

Activation swaps the symlink atomically and reloads the core — the previous release keeps serving until the new one is ready. Old releases are pruned automatically.

**Rollback:**

```bash
ln -sfn build/releases/<previous-tag> dist && yarn restart
```

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `BUILD_COMPRESS` | `brotli` | `brotli` · `gzip` · `both` · `none` |
| `BUILD_BROTLI_QUALITY` | `9` | 0–11 |
| `BUILD_GZIP_LEVEL` | `6` | 1–9 |

In development none of this is needed: client code is served by Vite with HMR.
"}},{"node":"deploy_prod","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Going Live","key":"deploy_prod","id":"deploy_prod","name":"deploy_prod","value":"## Going Live

### 1. DNS

Point each public domain (an `A` record) to the server's IP.

### 2. Install and start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alphabit-technology/loopar-framework.git loopar
cd loopar
yarn install
yarn build
yarn prod          # production mode + boot
yarn startup       # survive reboots
```

### 3. Create the tenant

From the TUI (`yarn start`, `n`) or the Tenant Manager. Set its **Domain** and save.

### 4. Run the install wizard

Open the **install link** the TUI prints for the tenant (`o`). Installs through a public IP or domain need that link — it carries a one-time token, so nobody else can claim the fresh site. The token stops working after the install.

### 5. Verify

```bash
yarn logs loopar-core                     # the core is up
curl -s localhost:2019/config/ | head     # Caddy has the routes
curl -I https://client.com                # the site answers over HTTPS
```

### 6. Back it up

Enable scheduled backups and a remote destination in **Backup Settings** — see [Backups](/backups).

### Updating later

```bash
git pull
yarn deps          # only when dependencies changed
yarn build
```

Then update the apps from each tenant's **App Manager** — schema changes apply per tenant, and a safety backup is taken before an app is updated.
"}},{"node":"deploy_db","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Databases","key":"deploy_db","id":"deploy_db","name":"deploy_db","value":"## Databases

Each tenant has a **completely separate database**; tenants can even use different engines.

| Tenant | Database | Use Case |
|--------|----------|----------|
| dev | SQLite | Quick development |
| client-a | MySQL | Production |
| client-b | PostgreSQL | Production, advanced features |

The install wizard asks for the **server connection** only and creates the database itself (its name is derived from the organization). The result is written to `sites/<tenant>/config/db.config.json`:

```json
{
  "dialect": "mysql",
  "connection": {
    "host": "localhost",
    "port": "3306",
    "user": "loopar",
    "password": "secure_password"
  },
  "database": "db_a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8"
}
```

PostgreSQL uses the same shape with `"dialect": "postgres"` (port 5432). Without a `db.config.json` the tenant runs on zero-config **SQLite** in `sites/<tenant>/database/`.

The database user needs permission to create databases (or create one beforehand and grant it all privileges):

```sql
CREATE USER 'loopar'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'secure_password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO 'loopar'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
```

### Isolation guarantees

- ✅ Tenants cannot read each other's data
- ✅ Credentials and secrets are per tenant
- ✅ Schema migrations run per tenant
- ✅ Backup and restore per tenant
"}},{"node":"deploy_apps","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Apps per Tenant","key":"deploy_apps","id":"deploy_apps","name":"deploy_apps","value":"## Apps per Tenant

Apps live once in `/apps` and are **installed per tenant** from each tenant's **App Manager**.

| Aspect | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| **Code** | Shared (from `/apps`) — one deploy updates it for everyone |
| **Schema & data** | Per tenant — applied when the tenant installs or updates the app |
| **Config** | Independent per tenant |
| **Users** | Separate per tenant |

When an app's files are newer than what a tenant has installed, the Debugger's Status panel reports a pending update for that tenant.

### Rules the installer enforces

- A safety backup of the tenant is taken before an app is installed or updated.
- An app can't take over records that belong to another installed app — except the core framework (`loopar`), which always installs over conflicts so nothing can block a framework update.
- Entity renames recorded in an app (`renames.json`) are replayed on every tenant when it updates.

### Common patterns

```
SaaS:    CRM app ──► company-a · company-b · company-c (one tenant each)
Agency:  client-a: Shop + Blog · client-b: CRM + Dashboards
Sites:   one tenant serving several websites (see Website)
```
"}},{"node":"deploy_server","element":"markdown","data":{"label":"Server","key":"deploy_server","id":"deploy_server","name":"deploy_server","value":"## Server Requirements

| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| **CPU** | 1 core | 2+ cores |
| **RAM** | 1 GB | 2+ GB |
| **Storage** | 10 GB SSD | 20+ GB SSD (uploads and backups grow) |
| **Node.js** | 22.22+ | Latest 22.x LTS |
| **OS** | Ubuntu 22.04+ | Ubuntu 24.04 |

All tenants share the core process, so adding a tenant adds memory for its data and caches, not a whole new process. Size the machine for the busiest tenants and the build (Vite needs more memory while `yarn build` runs).

## Firewall

```bash
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp    # SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp    # HTTP (certificates + redirect)
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp   # HTTPS
sudo ufw enable
```

Keep the core's port (3000 by default) and Caddy's Admin API (2019) closed to the outside: traffic must go through Caddy.

## The dev site

The dev site can manage every tenant (Tenant Manager, builds, core mode). Protect it accordingly: a strong Administrator password with two-factor authentication, and ideally no public domain — reach it through localhost, an SSH tunnel or a VPN. Website domains never expose a Desk (they answer 404 on `/desk`).
"}}]}]
